source.title: The Levers of Political Persuasion with Conversational AI
source.authors: Kobi Hackenburg; Ben M. Tappin; Luke Hewitt; Ed Saunders; Sid Black; Hause Lin; Catherine Fist; Helen Margetts; David G. Rand; Christopher Summerfield

record.file_problem: The text is the full paper; no garbling or cutoff is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: It extends the scale-to-performance question to political persuasion, a downstream behaviour, and reports how persuasion varies with effective pre-training compute. It does not measure language-model pretraining loss or test compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper reports no held-out cross-entropy loss, loss extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation results. The rows below concern only V6: persuasion as a downstream outcome. Scaling-law results cited from other work are not recorded as findings of this study.
record.test_reason: The study measures how a downstream capability, persuading humans in conversation, changes with log effective pre-training compute across 17 base LLMs. This bears on V6 in a new setting. It measures no pretraining loss, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that, holding post-training constant, larger models are more persuasive (about +1.6pp per order of magnitude). They also conclude that gains from post-training (up to 51%) and prompting (27%) exceed returns to scale, so near-future persuasive power will stem more from post-training and prompting than from scale or personalization.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses randomized human persuasion experiments and estimates persuasion against effective pre-training compute; it does not measure the original scaling-law outcome, held-out language-model loss.
record.method_sensitivity: The scale association differed by post-training group: it was positive for uniformly chat-tuned models but not reliable for developer post-trained models. The authors state that heterogeneous developer post-training may confound scale.
record.problems: The outcome is political persuasion rather than pretraining loss. Scale estimates for proprietary models are estimates, and the authors note that heterogeneous, opaque developer post-training confounds interpretation of scale in that group. The supplied text gives no numerical values for the linear-versus-GAM predictive comparison.

untested.parts: Prediction of downstream performance from pretraining loss. Downstream tasks other than political persuasion. Out-of-sample extrapolation of the persuasion curve: the authors' projection to 10×/100× compute is not checked.
Not tested: no pretraining loss is measured.
Not tested for loss exponents. Only linear versus GAM fits of persuasion are compared.

missing.what: Difference tests: GPT-4o (3/25) is more persuasive than the larger GPT-4.5 (p=.004) and Grok-3 (p<.001). This is non-monotonicity with scale among frontier models.
missing.locator: Results, Persuasive returns to model scale; SM 2.3

missing.what: Interaction showing the developer post-trained slope is lower than the chat-tuned slope: −1.41pp [−2.76, −0.13].
missing.locator: Results, Persuasive returns to model scale

missing.what: Same-scale GPT-4o deployments differ by +3.50pp because of post-training, exceeding the projected gain from 10× compute (+1.59pp) and 100× compute (+3.19pp).
missing.locator: Results, Persuasive returns to model scale; Discussion

missing.what: Claim accuracy rises with scale among chat-tuned models but varies widely among frontier models; GPT-4.5 is about as accurate as Llama3.1-8B.

record.verdict_notes: Persuasion is treated as a downstream capability for V6. The scale variable is effective compute, with Epoch AI estimates for proprietary models, so the developer-model results carry scale uncertainty. Rows r5–r8 should be recast as the difference-test comparisons. The linear-in-log fit is a regression of effect size, not a power-law loss fit.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss is measured against parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run loss fit is used to predict loss on larger runs.
No fixed-compute loss-minimising parameter/token allocation is measured.
No comparison of architecture depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No other modality or training-regime loss scaling is tested.
Tests political persuasion against effective pre-training compute, not other downstream tasks or prediction from pretraining loss.
The study compares linear and flexible fits for persuasion, but does not test setup-dependence of language-model loss exponents or compute-optimal splits.

relationships.condition: Pooled models and uniformly chat-tuned open models
relationships.reason: Persuasion rises roughly linearly in log compute (+1.59pp and +1.83pp per order of magnitude), and a linear fit is preferred to a flexible one (r1, r2, r4).
relationships.display_finding: Persuasion increased by 1.59 percentage points per compute order of magnitude for pooled models and 1.83 for uniformly chat-tuned open models, with linear fits preferred over flexible alternatives.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Pooled models and uniformly chat-tuned open models
source_check.reason: r1 and r2 show positive persuasion slopes of +1.59pp [1.07, 2.13] and +1.83pp [1.42, 2.25] per decade of compute. r4 confirms that the flexible fit does not improve predictive accuracy significantly.

relationships.condition: Developer post-trained frontier models with heterogeneous post-training
relationships.reason: There is no reliable scale slope (+0.32pp, CI spans 0), and it differs significantly from the chat-tuned slope. Larger GPT-4.5 and Grok-3 are less persuasive than GPT-4o (3/25). The trend therefore depends on post-training (r3; the comparisons are given in the text).
relationships.display_finding: The scale slope was +0.32 percentage points with a confidence interval of −1.18 to 1.85, and larger GPT-4.5 and Grok-3 were less persuasive than GPT-4o amid heterogeneous post-training.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Developer post-trained frontier models with heterogeneous post-training
source_check.reason: For this separately specified condition group, r3 explicitly reports no reliable positive scale association: +0.32pp [−1.18, 1.85]. Under the verdict rules, an absent effect receives challenges. Heterogeneous post-training limits causal interpretation of this result.
